ta-l1d9q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus opening Lombard's treatment of the distinction of persons (Distinctions 9–21), after the unity of essence. It treats first the distinct persons, then (Dist. 22 onward) the names signifying distinction and unity. The persons are treated first as to their distinction and then (Dist. 19 onward) as to their equality. Their distinction is treated first in the Son's generation, which distinguishes him from the Father, and then (Dist. 10 onward) in the Spirit's procession. Distinction 9 asserts the eternity of generation against Arius, whose argument ran: everything born at some time was not, the Son is born, so he is not coeternal. Thomas maps Lombard's refutations from Augustine (splendour is not later than fire; Christ is God's power and wisdom, which God never lacked), from Ambrose (Isa. 43:10; a Father who became Father would have changed; the generation is incomprehensible, so the Arian appeal to its unknown mode proves nothing), and from Hilary (an eternal Father implies an eternal generation; 'whatever is born began to be' holds only of what is born from one who does not always beget). He also notes Lombard's question whether the Son 'is always being born', 'has always been born', or 'will always be born'. Two inquiries are announced, on the Son's distinction from the Father and on eternity. The first has two articles: whether the Son can be called 'another' (alius) than the Father, and whether Father and Son can be called several eternals.
claims: The Son's eternal generation is defended against Arius's argument that whatever is born once was not.
'Whatever is born began to be' holds only of what is born from one who does not always beget.
The generation is incomprehensible, so arguments from its unknown mode prove nothing.

ta-l1d9q1-d1e181.summary: First objection that the Son is not other (alius) than the Father. According to Priscian, 'alius' is a relative signifying diversity of substance, and Father and Son are of one substance.
claims: Priscian: 'alius' signifies diversity of substance.

ta-l1d9q1-d1e184.summary: Second objection. The unity of substance prevents the Son from being called something else (aliud) than the Father, because of the diversity 'aliud' signifies. 'Alius' and 'aliud' differ only in mode of signifying, masculine and neuter, and mode of signifying does not change signification, so neither can he be called 'alius'.
claims: 'Alius' and 'aliud' differ only in grammatical gender.

ta-l1d9q1-d1e187.summary: Third objection. If the Son is called other than the Father because he is from the Father, then since the Father is from himself, the Father would be other than himself.
claims: Being from another is the ground of otherness.

ta-l1d9q1-d1e191.summary: Fourth objection. According to Porphyry, a property makes not 'otherness of thing' (alietas) but 'alteration' (alteritas), and the Father is distinguished from the Son only by a relative property. So he should be called 'alter', not 'alius'.
claims: Porphyry: properties make alteritas, not alietas.

ta-l1d9q1-d1e194.summary: Sed contra. When things are really distinct, one is another thing than the other. Father and Son are really distinct (Dist. 2), so the Father is another thing than the Son and can be called 'other' (alius); Augustine also says so in Lombard's text.
claims: Really distinct things are 'other' to one another.

ta-l1d9q1-d1e197.summary: Thomas's determination. In God there are three things, essence, person, and property, to which the three grammatical genders are suited. The neuter, formless and implying no distinction of sex, suits the common, undistinguished essence. The masculine, a distinct gender, suits the person, which is distinct and signified as something existing in the divine nature; the feminine is not used for persons because of its imperfection. The feminine suits the property, signified as form, and can suit the essence as signified as form. So because of the unity of essence the Father is not 'aliud' than the Son, but because of the distinction of person he is 'alius'. Thomas judges this more a fitting accommodation than an account of how the locution works. Better: the neuter is used substantively and so implies diversity simply and absolutely, which is diversity of essence, while masculine and feminine are used adjectivally and place their diversity on the personal terms in the proposition, as in 'the Son is other than the Father'.
claims: The Son is 'alius' but not 'aliud' than the Father.
Neuter used substantively implies diversity of essence; masculine used adjectivally implies diversity of the person it modifies.

ta-l1d9q1-d1e203.summary: Reply to the first objection. 'Alius' always signifies diversity of substance, but 'substance' is said in two ways: as essence, the Latin usage, or as the supposit of the essence, the thing of the nature in the first category, the Greeks' hypostasis. In the second sense Father and Son are not the same substance, since substance then signifies the person, and so the Son can be called 'alius'.
claims: 'Alius' signifies diversity of substance taken as hypostasis, not as essence.

ta-l1d9q1-d1e206.summary: Reply to the second objection. The neuter is used substantively, not the masculine. A substantive has its signification absolutely, while an adjective places its signification on a subject. What is said absolutely is understood of what is simply, as 'being' said absolutely signifies substance. Since otherness of essence is otherness simply, the substantival neuter implies otherness of essence. The masculine, used adjectivally, places otherness on its subject: with a personal term as its noun it signifies distinction of persons, so 'the Father is another (alius) than the Son' is true; with an essential term it signifies diversity of substance, so 'the Father is another God than the Son' is false. Likewise the neuter used adjectivally with a personal term implies otherness of person, as in 'the Father is another supposit (aliud suppositum) than the Son'. So the difference comes not from a change in signification but from what the signified otherness is referred to.
claims: The difference between 'alius' and 'aliud' lies in substantival vs. adjectival construal, not in signification.
'The Father is alius than the Son' is true; 'the Father is another God than the Son' is false.

ta-l1d9q1-d1e209.summary: Reply to the third objection. 'The Father is from himself' is improper and must be read negatively, as 'he is not from another', whereas 'the Son is from the Father' is proper. So the cases are not alike.
claims: 'The Father is a se' means only that he is not from another.

ta-l1d9q1-d1e213.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. In God a property is not merely a property but subsistent: paternity is the Father himself. So a property makes 'alius' more properly than 'alter' (treated more fully in Dist. 26).
claims: Divine properties are subsistent, so they make the persons alius, not merely alter.

ta-l1d9q1-d1e225.summary: First objection that Father and Son cannot be called several eternals, from the Athanasian Creed: 'and yet not three eternals'.
claims: The Athanasian Creed denies three eternals.

ta-l1d9q1-d1e231.summary: Second objection from Augustine: whatever is said of God absolutely (ad se) is predicated of the three in the singular, not the plural. 'Eternal' is said absolutely, not relatively.
claims: Absolute divine predicates are said in the singular of the three.

ta-l1d9q1-d1e237.summary: Third objection. As there is one deity of the three persons, there is one eternity, since eternity is the divine substance. 'Father and Son are several gods' cannot be said because of the unity of deity, so neither 'several eternals' because of the unity of eternity.
claims: Unity of eternity parallels unity of deity.

ta-l1d9q1-d1e241.summary: Sed contra from the Athanasian Creed: the three persons are coeternal. To the reply that 'God' is a substantive and 'eternal' an adjective that takes plural number from its supposits, it is objected that an adjective signifies by way of an accident and there are no accidents in God (Boethius: the other categories turn into substance in divine predication), so there can be no adjectives there.
claims: The three persons are coeternal.
Adjectives signify by way of accident.

ta-l1d9q1-d1e244.summary: Second sed contra. An adjective takes its number from its substantive, 'eternal' is an adjective, and Father and Son are several, so they should be called eternals.
claims: Adjectives take number from their substantives.

ta-l1d9q1-d1e247.summary: Thomas's determination. Substantives signify by way of substance and so signify their content absolutely; a substantive is plural only if its form is numbered. Adjectives signify by way of accident, which has no absolute being or unity, its being and unity depending on what it inheres in. Accidents are multiplied not by dividing a part of themselves, as species are by the division of matter into individuals, but by the division of their subjects: this whiteness differs from that one as it belongs to this subject or that. So adjectives are plural only on the side of their supposits. Terms signifying the substance substantively are not predicated in the plural of the three persons, since the signified form, the divine essence, is not divided. Terms signifying the substance adjectivally, as inhering or 'following the substance' (Damascene), are predicated in the plural because of the plurality of supposits. Among these there is an order. Verbs and participles signify by way of act, signified only as inhering, and should never be predicated in the singular. Adjectival names signify substance with quality, as grammarians say, and can more easily be predicated in the singular, especially since they can be substantivized, like 'eternal'. When a preposition expressing a relation of person to person is compounded with them, they are drawn more toward the supposit and must be predicated only in the plural, like 'coeternal'.
claims: Substantive essential terms are predicated of the three persons only in the singular; adjectival ones can be plural through the plurality of supposits.
Verbs and participles are always plural of the persons; adjectives like 'eternal' can be singular when substantivized.
Compounds expressing inter-personal relation, like 'coeternal', are always plural.

ta-l1d9q1-d1e250.summary: Reply to the first objection. If 'eternal' is taken substantively, it is predicated in the singular of the three, and this is Athanasius's sense. If taken adjectivally, it is predicated in the plural. 'Coeternal' must always be predicated in the plural because of the relation of person to person it implies.
claims: Athanasius's 'not three eternals' takes 'eternal' substantively.

ta-l1d9q1-d1e253.summary: Reply to the second objection. Adjectives have no number of themselves but from their supposits. So 'eternal', though not numbered of itself, since it is absolute, is predicated in the plural because of the plurality of supposits, which are relative.
claims: Absolute adjectives take plural number from relatively distinct supposits.

ta-l1d9q1-d1e256.summary: Reply to the third objection, following from the above. 'God' is not an adjective that takes number from another, as 'eternal' does, so it could be predicated in the plural only through a plurality of its own form, which is not to be posited in God.
claims: 'Deus' could be plural only by a plurality of deity, which does not exist.

ta-l1d9q1-d1e260.summary: Reply to the first sed contra. Although there is no accident in God in reality, something can be signified as adjacent to or following the substance in mode of signifying, and that is why there are adjectives in divine predication.
claims: Adjectives in divine names reflect mode of signifying, not real accidents.

ta-l1d9q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 9 opens Lombard's treatment of the distinct persons and places Distinction 9 as the defence of the Son's eternal generation against Arius, using Augustine, Ambrose, and Hilary. It announces inquiries into the distinction of Son from Father and into eternity.
claims: The Son's generation is eternal; Arius's argument from birth to beginning fails.

ta-l1d9q1-Dd1e173.summary: Article 1 asks whether the Son can be called 'other' (alius) than the Father. Thomas holds that the Son is 'alius' but not 'aliud' than the Father. He first relates the three grammatical genders to essence, person, and property, then explains the point more rigorously: the substantival neuter signifies diversity of essence absolutely, while the adjectival masculine places diversity on the personal term it modifies. 'Alius' implies diversity of substance only in the sense of hypostasis. 'The Father is from himself' is to be read negatively, and since divine properties are subsistent, they make the persons 'alius' rather than merely 'alter'.
claims: The Son is alius, not aliud, than the Father.
Substantival neuter implies diversity of essence; adjectival masculine implies diversity of person.

ta-l1d9q1-Dd1e217.summary: Article 2 asks whether Father and Son can be called several eternals. Thomas distinguishes substantives, which are plural only if their form is numbered, from adjectives, which take number from their supposits, as accidents are multiplied by their subjects. Substantive essential terms ('God') are predicated only in the singular. Adjectival terms can be plural: verbs and participles always, adjectives like 'eternal' plural when adjectival and singular when substantivized (Athanasius's 'not three eternals'). Relational compounds like 'coeternal' are always plural. Adjectives in God reflect mode of signifying, not real accidents.
claims: 'Eternal' is singular of the three when taken substantively and plural when taken adjectivally; 'coeternal' is always plural.
Essential substantives such as 'God' are never plural of the persons.

ta-l1d9q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 9 begins the treatment of the distinct persons with the Son's eternal generation and examines the language of his distinction from the Father. The Prooemium maps Lombard's refutation of Arius through Augustine, Ambrose, and Hilary. Article 1 holds that the Son is 'alius' (masculine, adjectival, bearing on the person) but not 'aliud' (neuter, substantival, implying diversity of essence) than the Father. It notes that 'alius' implies diversity of hypostasis and that subsistent divine properties make the persons 'alius'. Article 2 explains how essential terms take number: substantives remain singular because the divine form is one, while adjectives can be plural through the plurality of supposits. So 'eternal' is singular or plural depending on its construal, and 'coeternal' is always plural.
claims: The Son is alius but not aliud than the Father.
Essential substantives are singular of the persons; adjectives can be plural through the plurality of supposits.
'Coeternal' is always plural; 'eternal' is singular only when substantivized.
